title: (Sub)millimeter Stargazers
caption: The Milky Way over ALMA antennas, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The vast, bright ripple of the Milky Way slices the sky in two above Chile's Chajnantor plateau. Beneath its glow, a cluster of white antennas points upward, lit by a bright yellow light that tells technicians whether it is safe to approach. From the southern hemisphere, the rich center of our galaxy is often right overhead, stretching from horizon to horizon.

The antennas belong to ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, a giant interferometer of 66 antennas that work together across distances of up to 16 kilometers. ALMA observes light the eye cannot see, at wavelengths of around a millimeter, between infrared and radio. This light is given off by the coldest, most remote parts of the cosmos, such as clouds of gas and dust between the stars and the most ancient galaxies.
This light is heavily absorbed by water vapor, so telescopes must sit on very high, dry sites. At over 5000 meters, the plateau is ideal.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at the ALMA site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can gather far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way may look brighter and more detailed than it would to someone on the plateau.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Studying this cold, faint light lets ALMA explore how stars and planets form and change over time, revealing objects and processes that had never been seen before.
alt: The bright band of the Milky Way across the sky above a group of white dish antennas lit by a yellow light.
